instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: why branded clothes work for small shops
Audience: indie founders
Tone: natural
Words: ~100
output:
Branded clothes turn a vague "we exist" into something people can wear. A clean tee with your mark on the chest is a walking receipt—customers remember the shop because they saw the logo on a commute, not in an ad.

Start small. One well-cut shirt beats five mediocre colors. Print on fabric that feels good; cheap ink cracks after two washes and the brand looks cheap with it. Price for a thin margin, not a loss-leader race.

Use merch at events and in the bag with every order. Ask buyers what they actually want to wear. Then print that—not what looks clever in a moodboard.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: how to choose a merch printer
Audience: small ecommerce brands
Tone: practical
Words: ~90
output:
Ask for a sample of the exact blank you'll use. Photos hide thin fabric and muddy blacks. Check turnaround in writing, not in a chat promise.

Compare ink methods: screen print holds up for solid logos; DTG suits detailed art but can feel stiff if overdone. Get a quote that includes shipping and reprints for misprints—those "gotchas" wipe a launch margin.

If the printer won't share care labels or fabric specs, walk. Your customers will notice before you do.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: branded hoodies for winter pop-ups
Audience: streetwear founders
Tone: conversational
Words: ~85
output:
A hoodie at a winter pop-up does more than keep someone warm. It's the piece people keep wearing after the booth is packed. Go mid-weight—not a summer fleece pretending to be winter gear.

Keep the front graphic simple; sleeves and hoods eat detail. Offer two sizes that fit most bodies rather than eight that sit unsold. Let people try it on. Fit sells louder than a discount sticker.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: logo placement on apparel
Audience: designers working with brands
Tone: clear advice
Words: ~95
output:
Center-chest is safe; left-chest feels quieter and more "uniform." Oversized back prints read from across a room—great for events, noisy for office wear.

Measure from the collar, not from a flat sketch. Fabric stretch moves a logo half an inch in ways mockups never show. Leave breathing room around the mark; cramped art looks accidental.

Test one black and one light blank before you order a run. Contrast fails in person more often than on screen.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: sustainable fabric basics for merch
Audience: eco-curious brands
Tone: honest
Words: ~100
output:
"Sustainable" on a hangtag means little without specifics. Ask what the cotton is, where it's spun, and how the dye house treats wastewater. Organic cotton helps pesticide load; recycled polyester cuts virgin plastic but still sheds microfibers in the wash.

Pick one improvement you can prove—GOTS fabric, a repair policy, or fewer SKUs so less sits in landfill. Customers smell greenwash. A short, true sentence beats a paragraph of vibes.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: sizing charts that reduce returns
Audience: DTC apparel
Tone: practical
Words: ~80
output:
Publish measurements, not just S/M/L. Chest, length, and a note on fit (boxy vs slim) cut guesswork. Show a photo of the same person in two sizes if you can.

Update the chart when the blank supplier changes. One silent fabric swap can spike returns overnight. Link the chart from the product page and the cart—people check late.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: launching a second colorway
Audience: small clothing labels
Tone: natural
Words: ~75
output:
Don't launch five colors because the printer offered a deal. Launch the second color only after the first sells through without heavy discounting. Use leftover blanks for samples and photos, not for cluttering the shop.

Announce the new color with a real reason—season, restock feedback, a collaboration. Mystery drops work for some audiences; most shops do better with a clear "why now."

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: care labels customers actually read
Audience: apparel makers
Tone: helpful
Words: ~70
output:
Put wash temp and dry advice in plain words. "Cold wash, hang dry" beats a wall of symbols nobody learned. If the print cracks in a dryer, say so up front.

Short care notes in the package insert help too. People lose hangtags; they keep the shirt.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: photography tips for clothing product pages
Audience: solo founders
Tone: conversational
Words: ~90
output:
Natural light near a window beats a cheap ring light that blows out whites. Shoot the garment on a body and flat—shoppers need both. Keep backgrounds quiet so fabric texture shows.

One honest close-up of stitching or print edges builds more trust than ten filtered hero shots. Crop consistently across the catalog so scrolling feels calm, not chaotic.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: wholesale vs direct for branded tees
Audience: growing merch brands
Tone: clear
Words: ~95
output:
Wholesale gets you on more shelves; direct keeps your margin and your customer list. Many small brands do both: shops get a clean wholesale tier, and your site keeps exclusives or limited drops.

Don't undercut your wholesale partners on the same SKU without a plan. They notice. If you need a web-only deal, make it a different color or a bundle.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: morning routines that aren't performative
Audience: busy professionals
Tone: natural
Words: ~85
output:
You don't need a 5 a.m. cold plunge. Pick two anchors: water before coffee, and ten quiet minutes without a screen. That's enough to feel less yanked into the day.

If gym time won't fit, walk while you take one call. Protect sleep more fiercely than any productivity app. A rested Tuesday beats a heroic Monday that collapses.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: hosting friends without stress
Audience: home cooks
Tone: warm
Words: ~90
output:
Cook one dish you already know. Buy good bread and a simple salad. People remember how the room felt, not whether the sauce was plated like a magazine.

Clear a surface for coats and bags. Put music on before the first knock. Ask one person to bring dessert so you're not alone in the kitchen spiral.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: weekend reset for a small apartment
Audience: city renters
Tone: practical
Words: ~80
output:
Set a 45-minute timer. Surfaces first—counters, table, desk—then floors. Bag trash and recycling in one pass. Don't deep-clean the oven unless it's actually blocking you.

Open a window if you can. Fresh air makes a tidy room feel finished. Stop when the timer ends; leftover clutter can wait for next weekend.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: packing light for a three-day trip
Audience: frequent travelers
Tone: conversational
Words: ~85
output:
Wear your bulkiest shoes on the plane. Pack outfits that share the same bottoms. One sweater that layers beats three thin jackets fighting for space.

Put liquids in a clear pouch you can grab at security. Charge cables in a single zip bag so hotel nights aren't a scavenger hunt. Leave room for one thing you'll buy.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: making a small desk feel usable
Audience: remote workers
Tone: clear
Words: ~75
output:
One task light and a monitor at eye level matter more than desk gadgets. Keep only today's papers on the surface. Charge the phone out of arm's reach during deep work.

A small plant or a photo is fine; a shrine of sticky notes is not. Wipe the desk Friday so Monday doesn't start in last week's mess.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: choosing plants that survive neglect
Audience: new plant owners
Tone: honest
Words: ~70
output:
Start with pothos or snake plant. They forgive missed waterings better than fiddle-leaf figs. Put them where you already look—near the kettle or the desk—so you notice when leaves droop.

Overwatering kills more beginners than drought. When in doubt, wait two days.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: gift ideas that aren't clutter
Audience: thoughtful shoppers
Tone: natural
Words: ~80
output:
Consumables win: good coffee, a candle with a real scent, a jar of something homemade. Experiences work too—museum tickets, a class, a prepaid dinner.

If you give an object, make it something they'd buy twice: a sharp kitchen knife, wool socks, a notebook they'll actually fill. Skip novelty that dies in a drawer.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: quiet evenings without doomscrolling
Audience: anyone tired of phones
Tone: gentle
Words: ~75
output:
Charge the phone in another room after a set hour. Keep a book or a sketchpad where the couch is. Tea helps because it gives your hands a job.

You won't become a monk overnight. Aim for three evenings a week. The point is rest, not a perfect streak on an app.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: how to outline a blog post fast
Audience: content writers
Tone: practical
Words: ~90
output:
Write the question your reader is actually asking in one line. List three answers or steps. Under each, add one concrete example—a number, a tool, a mistake you've seen.

Draft the middle first; openings are easier once you know the point. Cut any paragraph that restates the previous one. End with what to do next, not a vague "in conclusion."

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: editing your own draft overnight
Audience: bloggers
Tone: natural
Words: ~85
output:
Sleep on it if you can. In the morning, read aloud. Wherever you stumble, the sentence is wrong. Kill throat-clearing first lines.

Check that every claim has a who/what/when nearby. Swap soft verbs for specific ones. Then stop—another hour of polish rarely adds as much as shipping and getting a real comment.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing product descriptions that sell
Audience: ecommerce copywriters
Tone: clear
Words: ~95
output:
Lead with what it does in daily life, not the material science lecture. "Keeps coffee hot through a long meeting" beats "double-wall vacuum insulation" alone—though specs belong lower on the page.

Name the fit, the weight, the care. Address the doubt you hear in support tickets. Short paragraphs; shoppers skim on phones.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: how to run a useful retrospective
Audience: small product teams
Tone: practical
Words: ~80
output:
Pick one project, not the whole quarter. Ask: what worked, what hurt, what we'll change. Write actions with owners and dates—complaints without owners are theater.

Keep it to 30 minutes. Ban blame hunting. Celebrate one specific win so people leave willing to be honest next time.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: onboarding a freelance designer
Audience: startup founders
Tone: conversational
Words: ~90
output:
Send brand files, three good examples, and three bad ones. State the deadline and the revision limit before work starts. Pay a kickoff portion so the project is real on both sides.

Give feedback in batches, not drip-by-drip midnight Slack. Point to the goal ("clearer hierarchy") more than taste adjectives ("make it pop").

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: batch-cooking for weeknights
Audience: busy households
Tone: helpful
Words: ~85
output:
Cook a pot of grains, a tray of roasted vegetables, and one protein on Sunday. Mix and match through Thursday; Friday can be takeout without guilt.

Use the same spices across dishes so the fridge doesn't become five unrelated cuisines. Label containers with the day. Future-you is tired and will not remember Tuesday's plan.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: setting boundaries on Slack
Audience: remote teams
Tone: honest
Words: ~75
output:
Status messages help: "deep work until 2, emergencies only." Mute channels that are FYI-only. Answer non-urgent threads in two daily windows instead of living in the sidebar.

Managers set the tone—if you praise midnight replies, you train midnight anxiety. Model the pace you want.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: capsule wardrobe starters
Audience: people tired of closet chaos
Tone: natural
Words: ~90
output:
Begin with neutrals you already wear: two bottoms, three tops, one jacket. Add one accent piece you love so the set doesn't feel like a uniform. Fit matters more than brand names.

Donate what you haven't worn in a year unless it's seasonal formalwear. Take a photo of outfits that worked; repeat them. Fashion thrives on boredom more than we admit.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: thrifting jackets that last
Audience: budget style seekers
Tone: practical
Words: ~80
output:
Check seams, zippers, and underarms. Smell the lining—some odors never leave. Prefer natural fibers you can tailor; cheap synthetics fight alterations.

Try it over a sweater you'll actually wear. If the shoulders sit wrong, walk away; that's hard to fix. A great thrift jacket costs less than fast fashion and looks less temporary.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: sneaker care basics
Audience: casual wearers
Tone: conversational
Words: ~70
output:
Knock dirt off outside before it grinds into the foam. Spot-clean with mild soap; avoid the washing machine unless the maker says it's safe. Rotate pairs so midsoles recover.

Replace laces when they fray—it's a five-dollar refresh that makes old shoes look intentional.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: building a lookbook on a phone
Audience: indie fashion brands
Tone: clear
Words: ~85
output:
Shoot the same location for a whole drop so the set feels coherent. Mix full-body and detail crops. Write one-line captions that name the piece, not a poem.

Export at web size; huge files slow the shop. Credit the model and photographer. A small lookbook shipped on time beats a perfect one that misses the season.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: customer emails that feel human
Audience: support for apparel brands
Tone: warm
Words: ~80
output:
Open with the specific issue: the size, the order number, the photo they sent. Say what you'll do next and when. Skip corporate fog like "we apologize for any inconvenience" unless you also fix something.

If you can't reprint, offer a clear choice—refund, store credit, or exchange. People want a path, not a vibe.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: photographing food for a recipe blog
Audience: home cooks who write
Tone: natural
Words: ~85
output:
Shoot near a window; turn off the overhead yellow light. Style with one prop—a napkin, a spoon—not a flea market on the table. Take the hero shot before anyone digs in, then a messy mid-bite shot for honesty.

Write the method as you cook once. Memory lies about salt and timing.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: starting a neighborhood walking habit
Audience: beginners
Tone: encouraging
Words: ~70
output:
Pick a loop you can finish in twenty minutes. Same time of day helps it stick. Leave the headphones home once a week so you notice the street.

Track streaks lightly; missing a day isn't failure. Rain walks with a jacket still count.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: decluttering digital files
Audience: freelancers
Tone: practical
Words: ~75
output:
Create a folder for this year and archive the rest in a zip you rarely open. Name files with dates first: 2026-08-client-invoice.pdf. Delete downloads older than 30 days after a quick scan.

Back up before you mass-delete. Regret is cheaper than lost contracts.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing a useful FAQ page
Audience: SaaS and shops
Tone: clear
Words: ~80
output:
Mine real support tickets. Answer the top ten in plain language. Link to the exact settings screen or policy section.

Keep answers short; link out for edge cases. Update the FAQ when you change pricing or shipping—stale FAQs create more tickets than they save.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: choosing fonts for a brand site
Audience: small business owners
Tone: practical
Words: ~90
output:
One display face and one readable body face are enough. Test body text at mobile size before you fall in love with a delicate serif. Check contrast on your real background color.

License the fonts properly; free personal licenses often block commercial sites. Consistency across site, packing slip, and social beats chasing trends every quarter.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: meal prep containers that don't leak
Audience: lunch packers
Tone: honest
Words: ~65
output:
Glass with a locking lid survives soup better than flimsy plastic. Test with water in the bag before you trust it on a commute. Leave headspace—hot food expands and pops seals.

Wash lids by hand if the dishwasher warps them. A warped lid is why "leakproof" fails.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: negotiating a small raise
Audience: individual contributors
Tone: grounded
Words: ~90
output:
List outcomes you owned: shipped projects, saved costs, mentored people. Ask for a number with a range, not "whatever feels fair." Practice out loud once so the first time isn't in the room.

If budget is frozen, ask what would unlock it and when to revisit. Get the next step in writing. Polite persistence beats a single dramatic speech.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: keeping houseplants alive while traveling
Audience: travelers with plants
Tone: helpful
Words: ~70
output:
Water thoroughly the morning you leave. Group plants away from AC blasts. For trips over ten days, ask a neighbor or use a simple drip bulb—don't invent a complex system you'll forget to reset.

Move sensitive plants out of harsh sun while you're gone; empty apartments get hotter than you think.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing alt text for product images
Audience: accessibility-minded shop owners
Tone: clear
Words: ~75
output: Describe what's unique: color, cut, material, what's in the frame. Skip "image of" and marketing fluff. If the image shows a stain detail or size comparison, say that—alt text is for people who can't see the photo, not for SEO stuffing.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: planning a pop-up booth layout
Audience: craft fair vendors
Tone: practical
Words: ~85
output:
Put your bestseller at eye level near the aisle. Leave a clear path so two people can browse without a traffic jam. Hide storage under the table with a clean cloth—visible chaos kills sales.

Keep checkout on one side with a small sign for prices. Test the setup at home with the same table width.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: finding angles for a saturated topic
Audience: bloggers
Tone: natural
Words: ~90
output:
Interview one practitioner. Use a local example. Argue a narrow claim ("three mistakes new thrifters make") instead of "the ultimate guide." Constraints create voice.

Read the top five results and note what they all repeat—then write the gap. Your draft should teach something those pages skip, even if it's small.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: using research without sounding academic
Audience: magazine-style writers
Tone: conversational
Words: ~80
output:
Put the human consequence first, then the study in a short clause. "Most people quit after week two (a 2023 habit study found the same pattern)" reads cleaner than a literature review opener.

Link or cite once. Don't stack three journals in one sentence unless your audience is researchers.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: headlines that set fair expectations
Audience: editors
Tone: clear
Words: ~70
output:
Promise the outcome the article delivers. Avoid clickbait that the body can't pay off. Numbers help when they're real: "seven packing rules" only if there are seven.

Test the headline against the last paragraph—if they disagree, fix one of them.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing about tools you haven't used long
Audience: tech explainers
Tone: honest
Words: ~85
output:
Say how long you tried it. Separate facts you verified from impressions. Compare to one familiar alternative instead of ranking the whole market.

Disclose affiliates. Readers forgive newness; they don't forgive fake expertise. Offer what to watch for in the first week so others can learn with you.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: soft CTAs in blog posts
Audience: content marketers
Tone: natural
Words: ~75
output:
Invite one next step that matches the article: a checklist download, a related guide, a product only if it's truly on-topic. Hard sells after a how-to feel like a bait switch.

Place the ask after value, not in the first paragraph. Respect the reader's time; they can smell desperation.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: revising AI-assisted drafts ethically
Audience: writers using assistants
Tone: grounded
Words: ~95
output:
Treat the model as a rough sketch. Add your examples, your numbers, your judgment. Cut stock phrases and empty transitions. Check facts you didn't personally verify.

Disclose AI help when your editor, client, or platform requires it. The goal is clearer writing in your voice—not fooling a detector. If a sentence could only exist to dodge software, delete it.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: seasonal window displays for a clothing shop
Audience: retail managers
Tone: practical
Words: ~80
output:
Change one focal piece and the props around it rather than rebuilding from scratch every week. Keep sightlines open so shoppers see inside. Lighting should flatter fabric, not cast harsh shadows on faces in the glass.

Update prices and sizes in the display so staff aren't apologizing at the door.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: denim fit guide for online shoppers
Audience: apparel brands
Tone: clear
Words: ~90
output:
Explain rise, leg shape, and stretch in everyday words. Show the same model in your two most popular fits. Note if the jean shrinks after wash—and by how much if you know.

Link a simple measuring guide. Returns drop when people can compare their favorite old pair to your chart before checkout.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: building a simple content calendar
Audience: solo creators
Tone: practical
Words: ~85
output:
Pick two themes a month and alternate. Batch research on Mondays, draft midweek, edit Fridays. Leave one open slot for timely posts so the calendar doesn't feel like a cage.

Review monthly: what got saves or replies, not just views. Drop formats that drain you even if they "perform." Sustainability includes yours.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: styling tips for video calls
Audience: remote workers
Tone: conversational
Words: ~70
output:
Solid colors beat tiny patterns that moiré on camera. Sit so the lens is at eye level. A lamp behind the laptop helps more than another productivity app.

Keep a blazer on the chair for sudden client calls. Comfort is fine; looking unfinished is optional.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing shipping policy pages people finish
Audience: ecommerce owners
Tone: clear
Words: ~80
output:
Lead with times and costs for the regions you actually ship. Say what happens on delays. Put returns in a linked section so the shipping page stays scannable.

Update holiday cutoffs in bold near the top every November. Buried policies create angry tickets and chargebacks.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: creating size-inclusive product photos
Audience: fashion brands
Tone: respectful
Words: ~85
output:
Show more than one body in the same garment when you can. Avoid cropping diversity into a token corner shot. Name the size worn in the caption.

Fit notes should help people choose, not moralize. Inclusive photos are part of product information—treat them with the same care as fabric specs.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: habit of weekly writing without burnout
Audience: aspiring bloggers
Tone: gentle
Words: ~75
output:
Lower the bar to a publishable minimum: 400 honest words beat an unfinished masterpiece. Keep a running list of titles so blank-page days have a starting line.

Skip a week when life spikes; restart without a guilt essay. Consistency is a pattern over months, not perfection every Sunday.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: choosing hangers that protect clothes
Audience: home organizers
Tone: practical
Words: ~65
output:
Velvet slim hangers save space and stop silk from slipping. Wooden hangers help structured jackets keep shape. Wire hangers leave dents—retire them.

Same hanger type makes the closet look calmer and makes gaps obvious when something's in the laundry.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: first pop-up checklist
Audience: new merch brands
Tone: practical
Words: ~90
output:
Confirm power, table size, and whether you need a permit. Pack a kit: tape, scissors, spare price tags, portable charger, bags, and a card-reader backup.

Print a simple size chart for the table. Bring more smalls and mediums than vanity sizes unless your audience skews otherwise. Cash a little float; card fees still surprise people.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: writing about fashion trends without hype
Audience: style writers
Tone: natural
Words: ~85
output:
Describe what people are actually wearing on the street or in your community. Name the practical reason a trend spreads—weather, work norms, price—before you call it a movement.

Credit subcultures when you borrow their language. Trends aren't neutral; say who gets priced out when a look goes mainstream.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: organizing a fabric scrap bin
Audience: sewers and DIY brands
Tone: helpful
Words: ~70
output:
Sort by fiber and size: patch-worthy, stuffing, trash. Label bags. Use scraps for pocket bags, cleaning cloths, or test stitches before you cut into new yardage.

Set a volume limit. When the bin overflows, decide—project or donate—before buying more fabric.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: cafe work sessions that stay productive
Audience: freelancers
Tone: conversational
Words: ~75
output:
Pick a task before you sit down. Buy something and don't camp for six hours on one tea. Noise-canceling helps; so does facing away from the door if you're distractible.

Leave when the work unit ends. Cafes are for sprints, not for building a second office without rent.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: plain language in customer docs
Audience: technical writers
Tone: clear
Words: ~80
output:
Short sentences help people under stress. Put the action first: "Click Save," not "It is recommended that users proceed to save." Cut jargon or define it once.

Test with someone outside the team. If they hesitate, the sentence failed—not the reader.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: why examples beat abstractions in how-tos
Audience: educators and bloggers
Tone: natural
Words: ~85
output:
"Use strong verbs" means little until you show "walked" versus "went." One worked example teaches faster than three principles. Keep the example in the reader's world—their tools, their constraints.

Then restate the rule in a single line they can screenshot.

instruction: Write a blog draft on the topic. Match the audience and tone. Return only the draft.
input:
Topic: citing sources in a blog without killing flow
Audience: nonfiction writers
Tone: practical
Words: ~75
output:
Use a short marker in the sentence and a Sources list at the end. Link the title people can recognize. Don't dump URLs mid-paragraph.

Gretel began to cry and said: ‘How are we to get out of the forest now?’ But Hansel comforted her and said: ‘Just wait a little, until the moon has risen, and then we will soon find the way.’ And when the full moon had risen, Hansel took his little sister by the hand, and followed the pebbles which shone like newly-coined silver pieces, and showed them the way.

output: His life falls naturally into three periods, each of which singularly enough constitutes a distinct and important era in the history of Florence. His youth was concurrent with the greatness of Florence as an Italian power under the guidance of Lorenzo de’ Medici, Il Magnifico. The downfall of the Medici in Florence occurred in 1494, in which year Machiavelli entered the public service. During his official career Florence was free under the government of a Republic, which lasted until 1512, when the Medici returned to power, and Machiavelli lost his office. The Medici again ruled Florence from 1512 until 1527, when they were once more driven out. This was the period of Machiavelli’s literary activity and increasing influence; but he died, within a few weeks of the expulsion of the Medici, on 22nd June 1527, in his fifty-eighth year, without having regained office.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Although there is little recorded of the youth of Machiavelli, the Florence of those days is so well known that the early environment of this representative citizen may be easily imagined. Florence has been described as a city with two opposite currents of life, one directed by the fervent and austere Savonarola, the other by the splendour-loving Lorenzo. Savonarola’s influence upon the young Machiavelli must have been slight, for although at one time he wielded immense power over the fortunes of Florence, he only furnished Machiavelli with a subject of a gibe in The Prince, where he is cited as an example of an unarmed prophet who came to a bad end. Whereas the magnificence of the Medicean rule during the life of Lorenzo appeared to have impressed Machiavelli strongly, for he frequently recurs to it in his writings, and it is to Lorenzo’s grandson that he dedicates The Prince.

output: The second period of Machiavelli’s life was spent in the service of the free Republic of Florence, which flourished, as stated above, from the expulsion of the Medici in 1494 until their return in 1512. After serving four years in one of the public offices he was appointed Chancellor and Secretary to the Second Chancery, the Ten of Liberty and Peace. Here we are on firm ground when dealing with the events of Machiavelli’s life, for during this time he took a leading part in the affairs of the Republic, and we have its decrees, records, and dispatches to guide us, as well as his own writings. A mere recapitulation of a few of his transactions with the statesmen and soldiers of his time gives a fair indication of his activities, and supplies the sources from which he drew the experiences and characters which illustrate The Prince.

Various mental influences were at work during its composition; its title and patron were changed; and for some unknown reason it was finally dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici. Although Machiavelli discussed with Casavecchio whether it should be sent or presented in person to the patron, there is no evidence that Lorenzo ever received or even read it: he certainly never gave Machiavelli any employment. Although it was plagiarized during Machiavelli’s lifetime, The Prince was never published by him, and its text is still disputable.

And of my loyalty none could doubt, because having always kept faith I could not now learn how to break it; for he who has been faithful and honest, as I have, cannot change his nature; and my poverty is a witness to my honesty.”

These and several minor works occupied him until the year 1518, when he accepted a small commission to look after the affairs of some Florentine merchants at Genoa. In 1519 the Medicean rulers of Florence granted a few political concessions to her citizens, and Machiavelli with others was consulted upon a new constitution under which the Great Council was to be restored; but on one pretext or another it was not promulgated.

output: In 1520 the Florentine merchants again had recourse to Machiavelli to settle their difficulties with Lucca, but this year was chiefly remarkable for his re-entry into Florentine literary society, where he was much sought after, and also for the production of his “Art of War.” It was in the same year that he received a commission at the instance of Cardinal de’ Medici to write the “History of Florence,” a task which occupied him until 1525. His return to popular favour may have determined the Medici to give him this employment, for an old writer observes that “an able statesman out of work, like a huge whale, will endeavour to overturn the ship unless he has an empty cask to play with.”

output: When the “History of Florence” was finished, Machiavelli took it to Rome for presentation to his patron, Giuliano de’ Medici, who had in the meanwhile become pope under the title of Clement VII. It is somewhat remarkable that, as, in 1513, Machiavelli had written The Prince for the instruction of the Medici after they had just regained power in Florence, so, in 1525, he dedicated the “History of Florence” to the head of the family when its ruin was now at hand. In that year the battle of Pavia destroyed the French rule in Italy, and left Francis I a prisoner in the hands of his great rival, Charles V. This was followed by the sack of Rome, upon the news of which the popular party at Florence threw off the yoke of the Medici, who were once more banished.

output: No one can say where the bones of Machiavelli rest, but modern Florence has decreed him a stately cenotaph in Santa Croce, by the side of her most famous sons; recognizing that, whatever other nations may have found in his works, Italy found in them the idea of her unity and the germs of her renaissance among the nations of Europe. Whilst it is idle to protest against the world-wide and evil signification of his name, it may be pointed out that the harsh construction of his doctrine which this sinister reputation implies was unknown to his own day, and that the researches of recent times have enabled us to interpret him more reasonably. It is due to these inquiries that the shape of an “unholy necromancer,” which so long haunted men’s vision, has begun to fade.

Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Although the light of almost four centuries has been focused on The Prince, its problems are still debatable and interesting, because they are the eternal problems between the ruled and their rulers. Such as they are, its ethics are those of Machiavelli’s contemporaries; yet they cannot be said to be out of date so long as the governments of Europe rely on material rather than on moral forces. Its historical incidents and personages become interesting by reason of the uses which Machiavelli makes of them to illustrate his theories of government and conduct.

Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Leaving out of consideration those maxims of state which still furnish some European and eastern statesmen with principles of action, The Prince is bestrewn with truths that can be proved at every turn. Men are still the dupes of their simplicity and greed, as they were in the days of Alexander VI. The cloak of religion still conceals the vices which Machiavelli laid bare in the character of Ferdinand of Aragon. Men will not look at things as they really are, but as they wish them to be—and are ruined. In politics there are no perfectly safe courses; prudence consists in choosing the least dangerous ones. Then—to pass to a higher plane—Machiavelli reiterates that, although crimes may win an empire, they do not win glory. Necessary wars are just wars, and the arms of a nation are hallowed when it has no other resource but to fight.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

output: It is the cry of a far later day than Machiavelli’s that government should be elevated into a living moral force, capable of inspiring the people with a just recognition of the fundamental principles of society; to this “high argument” The Prince contributes but little. Machiavelli always refused to write either of men or of governments otherwise than as he found them, and he writes with such skill and insight that his work is of abiding value. But what invests The Prince with more than a merely artistic or historical interest is the incontrovertible truth that it deals with the great principles which still guide nations and rulers in their relationship with each other and their neighbours.

output: But the difficulties occur in a new principality. And firstly, if it be not entirely new, but is, as it were, a member of a state which, taken collectively, may be called composite, the changes arise chiefly from an inherent difficulty which there is in all new principalities; for men change their rulers willingly, hoping to better themselves, and this hope induces them to take up arms against him who rules: wherein they are deceived, because they afterwards find by experience they have gone from bad to worse. This follows also on another natural and common necessity, which always causes a new prince to burden those who have submitted to him with his soldiery and with infinite other hardships which he must put upon his new acquisition.

And if another should allege the pledge which the king had given to the Pope that he would assist him in the enterprise, in exchange for the dissolution of his marriage and for the cap to Rouen, to that I reply what I shall write later on concerning the faith of princes, and how it ought to be kept.

output: I answer that the principalities of which one has record are found to be governed in two different ways; either by a prince, with a body of servants, who assist him to govern the kingdom as ministers by his favour and permission; or by a prince and barons, who hold that dignity by antiquity of blood and not by the grace of the prince. Such barons have states and their own subjects, who recognize them as lords and hold them in natural affection. Those states that are governed by a prince and his servants hold their prince in more consideration, because in all the country there is no one who is recognized as superior to him, and if they yield obedience to another they do it as to a minister and official, and they do not bear him any particular affection.

Such men, for the reasons given, can open the way into the state and render the victory easy; but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties, both from those who have assisted you and from those you have crushed. Nor is it enough for you to have exterminated the family of the prince, because the lords that remain make themselves the heads of fresh movements against you, and as you are unable either to satisfy or exterminate them, that state is lost whenever time brings the opportunity.

Hence arose those frequent rebellions against the Romans in Spain, France, and Greece, owing to the many principalities there were in these states, of which, as long as the memory of them endured, the Romans always held an insecure possession; but with the power and long continuance of the empire the memory of them passed away, and the Romans then became secure possessors. And when fighting afterwards amongst themselves, each one was able to attach to himself his own parts of the country, according to the authority he had assumed there; and the family of the former lord being exterminated, none other than the Romans were acknowledged.

Because such a government, being created by the prince, knows that it cannot stand without his friendship and interest, and does its utmost to support him; and therefore he who would keep a city accustomed to freedom will hold it more easily by the means of its own citizens than in any other way.

Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: But when cities or countries are accustomed to live under a prince, and his family is exterminated, they, being on the one hand accustomed to obey and on the other hand not having the old prince, cannot agree in making one from amongst themselves, and they do not know how to govern themselves. For this reason they are very slow to take up arms, and a prince can gain them to himself and secure them much more easily. But in republics there is more vitality, greater hatred, and more desire for vengeance, which will never permit them to allow the memory of their former liberty to rest; so that the safest way is to destroy them or to reside there.

Topic: leadership: entirely, always, paths
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Let no one be surprised if, in speaking of entirely new principalities as I shall do, I adduce the highest examples both of prince and of state; because men, walking almost always in paths beaten by others, and following by imitation their deeds, are yet unable to keep entirely to the ways of others or attain to the power of those they imitate. A wise man ought always to follow the paths beaten by great men, and to imitate those who have been supreme, so that if his ability does not equal theirs, at least it will savour of it. Let him act like the clever archers who, designing to hit the mark which yet appears too far distant, and knowing the limits to which the strength of their bow attains, take aim much higher than the mark, not to reach by their strength or arrow to so great a height, but to be able with the aid of so high an aim to hit the mark they wish to reach.

Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: I say, therefore, that in entirely new principalities, where there is a new prince, more or less difficulty is found in keeping them, accordingly as there is more or less ability in him who has acquired the state. Now, as the fact of becoming a prince from a private station presupposes either ability or fortune, it is clear that one or other of these things will mitigate in some degree many difficulties. Nevertheless, he who has relied least on fortune is established the strongest. Further, it facilitates matters when the prince, having no other state, is compelled to reside there in person.

Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: It was necessary, therefore, to Moses that he should find the people of Israel in Egypt enslaved and oppressed by the Egyptians, in order that they should be disposed to follow him so as to be delivered out of bondage. It was necessary that Romulus should not remain in Alba, and that he should be abandoned at his birth, in order that he should become King of Rome and founder of the fatherland. It was necessary that Cyrus should find the Persians discontented with the government of the Medes, and the Medes soft and effeminate through their long peace. Theseus could not have shown his ability had he not found the Athenians dispersed. These opportunities, therefore, made those men fortunate, and their high ability enabled them to recognize the opportunity whereby their country was ennobled and made famous.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Topic: prudence: force, necessary, whether
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: It is necessary, therefore, if we desire to discuss this matter thoroughly, to inquire whether these innovators can rely on themselves or have to depend on others: that is to say, whether, to consummate their enterprise, have they to use prayers or can they use force? In the first instance they always succeed badly, and never compass anything; but when they can rely on themselves and use force, then they are rarely endangered. Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Besides the reasons mentioned, the nature of the people is variable, and whilst it is easy to persuade them, it is difficult to fix them in that persuasion. And thus it is necessary to take such measures that, when they believe no longer, it may be possible to make them believe by force.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed they could not have enforced their constitutions for long—as happened in our time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined with his new order of things immediately the multitude believed in him no longer, and he had no means of keeping steadfast those who believed or of making the unbelievers to believe. Therefore such as these have great difficulties in consummating their enterprise, for all their dangers are in the ascent, yet with ability they will overcome them; but when these are overcome, and those who envied them their success are exterminated, they will begin to be respected, and they will continue afterwards powerful, secure, honoured, and happy.

Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: To these great examples I wish to add a lesser one; still it bears some resemblance to them, and I wish it to suffice me for all of a like kind: it is Hiero the Syracusan. This man rose from a private station to be Prince of Syracuse, nor did he, either, owe anything to fortune but opportunity; for the Syracusans, being oppressed, chose him for their captain, afterwards he was rewarded by being made their prince. He was of so great ability, even as a private citizen, that one who writes of him says he wanted nothing but a kingdom to be a king. This man abolished the old soldiery, organized the new, gave up old alliances, made new ones; and as he had his own soldiers and allies, on such foundations he was able to build any edifice: thus, whilst he had endured much trouble in acquiring, he had but little in keeping.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Concerning these two methods of rising to be a prince by ability or fortune, I wish to adduce two examples within our own recollection, and these are Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by proper means and with great ability, from being a private person rose to be Duke of Milan, and that which he had acquired with a thousand anxieties he kept with little trouble. On the other hand, Cesare Borgia, called by the people Duke Valentino, acquired his state during the ascendancy of his father, and on its decline he lost it, notwithstanding that he had taken every measure and done all that ought to be done by a wise and able man to fix firmly his roots in the states which the arms and fortunes of others had bestowed on him.

If, therefore, all the steps taken by the duke be considered, it will be seen that he laid solid foundations for his future power, and I do not consider it superfluous to discuss them, because I do not know what better precepts to give a new prince than the example of his actions; and if his dispositions were of no avail, that was not his fault, but the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune.

Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: But let us return whence we started. I say that the duke, finding himself now sufficiently powerful and partly secured from immediate dangers by having armed himself in his own way, and having in a great measure crushed those forces in his vicinity that could injure him if he wished to proceed with his conquest, had next to consider France, for he knew that the king, who too late was aware of his mistake, would not support him. And from this time he began to seek new alliances and to temporize with France in the expedition which she was making towards the kingdom of Naples against the Spaniards who were besieging Gaeta. It was his intention to secure himself against them, and this he would have quickly accomplished had Alexander lived.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.
input:
Topic: states: although, prince, private
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Although a prince may rise from a private station in two ways, neither of which can be entirely attributed to fortune or genius, yet it is manifest to me that I must not be silent on them, although one could be more copiously treated when I discuss republics. These methods are when, either by some wicked or nefarious ways, one ascends to the principality, or when by the favour of his fellow-citizens a private person becomes the prince of his country. And speaking of the first method, it will be illustrated by two examples—one ancient, the other modern—and without entering further into the subject, I consider these two examples will suffice those who may be compelled to follow them.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.
input:
Topic: states: ought, injuries, benefits
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Hence it is to be remarked that, in seizing a state, the usurper ought to examine closely into all those injuries which it is necessary for him to inflict, and to do them all at one stroke so as not to have to repeat them daily; and thus by not unsettling men he will be able to reassure them, and win them to himself by benefits. He who does otherwise, either from timidity or evil advice, is always compelled to keep the knife in his hand; neither can he rely on his subjects, nor can they attach themselves to him, owing to their continued and repeated wrongs. For injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.
input:
Topic: power: favour, principality, people
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~120
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: But coming to the other point—where a leading citizen becomes the prince of his country, not by wickedness or any intolerable violence, but by the favour of his fellow citizens—this may be called a civil principality: nor is genius or fortune altogether necessary to attain to it, but rather a happy shrewdness. I say then that such a principality is obtained either by the favour of the people or by the favour of the nobles. Because in all cities these two distinct parties are found, and from this it arises that the people do not wish to be ruled nor oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles wish to rule and oppress the people; and from these two opposite desires there arises in cities one of three results, either a principality, self-government, or anarchy.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.
input:
Topic: states: people, prince, becomes
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Therefore, one who becomes a prince through the favour of the people ought to keep them friendly, and this he can easily do seeing they only ask not to be oppressed by him. But one who, in opposition to the people, becomes a prince by the favour of the nobles, ought, above everything, to seek to win the people over to himself, and this he may easily do if he takes them under his protection. Because men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor; thus the people quickly become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to the principality by their favours; and the prince can win their affections in many ways, but as these vary according to the circumstances one cannot give fixed rules, so I omit them; but, I repeat, it is necessary for a prince to have the people friendly, otherwise he has no security in adversity.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Topic: leadership: always, people, cities
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: The cities of Germany are absolutely free, they own but little country around them, and they yield obedience to the emperor when it suits them, nor do they fear this or any other power they may have near them, because they are fortified in such a way that every one thinks the taking of them by assault would be tedious and difficult, seeing they have proper ditches and walls, they have sufficient artillery, and they always keep in public depots enough for one year’s eating, drinking, and firing. And beyond this, to keep the people quiet and without loss to the state, they always have the means of giving work to the community in those labours that are the life and strength of the city, and on the pursuit of which the people are supported; they also hold military exercises in repute, and moreover have many ordinances to uphold them.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.
input:
Topic: prudence: prince, subjects, therefore
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Therefore, a prince who has a strong city, and had not made himself odious, will not be attacked, or if any one should attack he will only be driven off with disgrace; again, because that the affairs of this world are so changeable, it is almost impossible to keep an army a whole year in the field without being interfered with. And whoever should reply: If the people have property outside the city, and see it burnt, they will not remain patient, and the long siege and self-interest will make them forget their prince; to this I answer that a powerful and courageous prince will overcome all such difficulties by giving at one time hope to his subjects that the evil will not be for long, at another time fear of the cruelty of the enemy, then preserving himself adroitly from those subjects who seem to him to be too bold.

instruction: Write a short essay paragraph on the topic in clear natural prose. Return only the paragraph.

Topic: states: therefore, prince, spirits
Audience: general readers
Tone: natural classic clarity
Words: ~160
Source style: public-domain human prose (Niccolò Machiavelli)
output: Further, the enemy would naturally on his arrival at once burn and ruin the country at the time when the spirits of the people are still hot and ready for the defence; and, therefore, so much the less ought the prince to hesitate; because after a time, when spirits have cooled, the damage is already done, the ills are incurred, and there is no longer any remedy; and therefore they are so much the more ready to unite with their prince, he appearing to be under obligations to them now that their houses have been burnt and their possessions ruined in his defence. For it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they confer as much as by those they receive. Therefore, if everything is well considered, it will not be difficult for a wise prince to keep the minds of his citizens steadfast from first to last, when he does not fail to support and defend them.

These mothers, instead of being able to work for their honest livelihood, are forced to employ all their time in stroling to beg sustenance for their helpless infants who, as they grow up, either turn thieves for want of work, or leave their dear native country, to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or sell themselves to the Barbadoes.

It is true, a child just dropt from its dam, may be supported by her milk, for a solar year, with little other nourishment: at most not above the value of two shillings, which the mother may certainly get, or the value in scraps, by her lawful occupation of begging; and it is exactly at one year old that I propose to provide for them in such a manner, as, instead of being a charge upon their parents, or the parish, or wanting food and raiment for the rest of their lives, they shall, on the contrary, contribute to the feeding, and partly to the clothing of many thousands.

Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.

Words: ~160

output: Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

Then he was a masterful dog, and what made him dangerous was the fact that the club of the man in the red sweater had knocked all blind pluck and rashness out of his desire for mastery. The rabbit sped down the river, turned off into a small creek, up the frozen bed of which it held steadily. It ran lightly on the surface of the snow, while the dogs ploughed through by main strength. Buck led the pack, sixty strong, around bend after bend, but he could not gain. He lay down low to the race, whining eagerly, his splendid body flashing forward, leap by leap, in the wan white moonlight.
